title: Ἀπηλεγέως
about: Achilles answers Odysseus bluntly. He hates a man who hides one thing in his mind and says another, and he does not think Agamemnon or the Danaans will persuade him: the fighter and the idler meet the same fate, and he has toiled for nothing, laying waste cities and handing the spoil to Agamemnon, who kept most of it and then took Achilles’ own prize. Let Agamemnon enjoy the woman and look to the ships himself; his wall and ditch cannot stop Hector, who never ventured far from Troy’s walls while Achilles fought. Tomorrow Achilles will sail, and on the third day he could be in Phthia. He rejects every gift, the daughter of Agamemnon included, for no wealth is worth his life, and his mother Thetis has told him of two paths, a short life with unfailing fame or a long one with none. He would advise all to sail home, tells the envoys to carry his answer to the chiefs, and says Phoenix may stay the night and follow him tomorrow if he wishes, but not by force.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: The formula that opens a reply: ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ with προσέφη ‘addressed’, and the stock epithet πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’, where πόδας is an accusative of respect (‘swift as to his feet’). The epithet is translated every time. The speech itself begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ
χρὴ μὲν δὴ τὸν μῦθον ἀπηλεγέως ἀποειπεῖν,
ᾗ περ δὴ φρονέω τε καὶ ὡς τετελεσμένον ἔσται,
ὡς μή μοι τρύζητε παρήμενοι ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος.
sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
it is necessary indeed the word bluntly to speak out,
in the way that I both think and as it will be accomplished,
so that you not murmur at me, sitting beside, one from one side, another from another.
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, I must speak my mind bluntly, just as I think it and as it will be carried out, so that you do not sit beside me and murmur at me, one from one side and another from another.
sentences.n: διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ is a whole-line vocative: διογενής ‘Zeus-sprung’, Λαερτιάδης ‘son of Laertes’ (a patronymic) and πολυμήχανος ‘many-devising’. The same line addresses Odysseus at 2.173. ἀπηλεγέως ‘bluntly’ is rare and its origin is uncertain (it is usually linked with ἀλέγω ‘care for’, so ‘without regard’), and ‘bluntly’ is the traditional sense. ἀποειπεῖν is the infinitive of ἀπεῖπον ‘speak out’, after χρή ‘it is necessary’. τρύζητε, from τρύζω ‘murmur, grumble’, is a subjunctive in a purpose clause with ὡς μή; ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is ‘one from one side, another from another’. The edition prints no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν
ὅς χ’ ἕτερον μὲν κεύθῃ ἐνὶ φρεσίν, ἄλλο δὲ εἴπῃ.
sentences.l:
For hateful to me is that man, just like the gates of Hades,
who one thing hides in his mind, and another says.
sentences.i: For that man is as hateful to me as the gates of Hades who hides one thing in his mind and says another.
sentences.n: ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν ‘just like the gates of Hades’: ὁμῶς ‘alike’ takes the dative πύλῃσιν (epic -ῃσιν), and Ἀΐδαο is the epic genitive of Ἀΐδης. The relative clause ὅς χ’ … κεύθῃ … εἴπῃ is general, ‘whoever hides … and says’, with χ’ for κε and subjunctives; ἕτερον … ἄλλο is ‘one thing … another’. Achilles names no one yet.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐρέω ὥς μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα·
sentences.l: But I shall say as it seems to me to be best.
sentences.i: But I will say it as it seems best to me.
sentences.n: ἐρέω ‘I shall say’ is the future of λέγω in its epic form, and ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα is ‘it seems to be best’. The ano teleia leads into the statement that follows (the English closes with a full stop, as it does for the same words where they first stand).

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ ἔμεγ’ Ἀτρεΐδην Ἀγαμέμνονα πεισέμεν οἴω
οὔτ’ ἄλλους Δαναούς, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἄρα τις χάρις ἦεν
μάρνασθαι δηΐοισιν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσι νωλεμὲς αἰεί.
sentences.l:
Neither me will Atreus’-son Agamemnon persuade, I think,
nor the other Danaans, since there was, it seems, no gratitude
in fighting against hostile men unceasingly, always.
sentences.i: I do not think that Agamemnon, the son of Atreus, will persuade me, nor will the other Danaans, since it seems that there was no gratitude for fighting hostile men without pause, forever.
sentences.n: πεισέμεν is the future infinitive of πείθω (Attic πείσειν), governed by οἴω ‘I think’ (οἴομαι), with Ἀτρεΐδην Ἀγαμέμνονα and ἄλλους Δαναούς as its two subjects in the accusative and ἔμεγ’ its object; ἔμεγ’ is ἐμέ γε. Ἀτρεΐδην is the patronymic ‘son of Atreus’, here Agamemnon. ἦεν is the imperfect ‘was’, and with ἄρα it marks something now seen to be so: ‘it turns out there was no χάρις’, here the gratitude owed for service. δηΐοισιν is the epic dative plural of δήϊος ‘hostile’; νωλεμές is the adverb ‘without pause’.

sentences.t: ἴση μοῖρα μένοντι καὶ εἰ μάλα τις πολεμίζοι·
sentences.l: An equal portion for the one who stays, even if one fights very hard;
sentences.i: The fate is the same for the man who stays behind and for the one who fights hard;
sentences.n: μένοντι ‘to the one who stays’, that is, who holds back from the fighting, balances the clause about the man who fights. ἴση μοῖρα is ‘an equal portion’ (μοῖρα, a share or lot, is ‘fate’ in the reading layer), and the next two lines say what the portion is: honour and death. εἰ μάλα τις πολεμίζοι is a general supposition with the optative, ‘even if one fights very hard’.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ ἰῇ τιμῇ ἠμὲν κακὸς ἠδὲ καὶ ἐσθλός·
sentences.l: and in one honour both the base man and the good:
sentences.i: and base and good alike are held in one honour;
sentences.n: ἰῇ is the epic feminine dative of εἷς ‘one’ (Attic μιᾷ); ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ καὶ is ‘both … and’. κακός and ἐσθλός said of men in battle are the coward (‘base’) and the brave man (‘good’).

sentences.t: κάτθαν’ ὁμῶς ὅ τ’ ἀεργὸς ἀνὴρ ὅ τε πολλὰ ἐοργώς.
sentences.l: Died alike both the idle man and the one who has done much.
sentences.i: The idle man dies just as the man of many deeds does.
sentences.n: κάτθαν’ is κάτθανε ‘died’ (from καταθνῄσκω, with the preverb joined on and no augment), elided before ὁμῶς. It is a gnomic aorist, a general truth put in a past tense, so the reading layer has the present. ὅ τ’ … ὅ τε: the article as a demonstrative, ‘the one … and the one’. ἐοργώς is the perfect participle of ἔρδω ‘do’ with the epic reduplication, ‘one who has done much’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί μοι περίκειται, ἐπεὶ πάθον ἄλγεα θυμῷ
αἰεὶ ἐμὴν ψυχὴν παραβαλλόμενος πολεμίζειν.
sentences.l:
Nor is anything left over for me, since I suffered pains in my heart,
always my life staking to fight.
sentences.i: Nothing is left over for me, since I suffered pains at heart, always risking my life in the fight.
sentences.n: περίκειται, from περίκειμαι ‘lie around, remain over’, says that no surplus remains to show for his labour; the word is unusual and the sense is taken from the verb. πάθον is the unaugmented aorist of πάσχω, ‘I suffered’, and ἄλγεα ‘pains’ is the object. παραβαλλόμενος, from παραβάλλομαι ‘put alongside, stake, hazard’, takes ψυχήν, which is ‘life’ when it is what a man stakes; πολεμίζειν is an infinitive of purpose, ‘in order to fight’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὄρνις ἀπτῆσι νεοσσοῖσι προφέρῃσι
μάστακ’ ἐπεί κε λάβῃσι, κακῶς δ’ ἄρα οἱ πέλει αὐτῇ,
sentences.l:
As a bird to unfledged chicks brings forward
a morsel, whenever she has got it, and it goes ill with herself,
sentences.i: As a bird brings a morsel to her unfledged chicks whenever she has got hold of one, though it goes ill with herself,
sentences.n: A simile begins, ὡς … ὥς; the application is in the next unit. ἀπτῆσι ‘unfledged’ (unable yet to fly) and νεοσσοῖσι ‘chicks’ are datives; προφέρῃσι ‘brings forward’ is a subjunctive in -ῃσι(ν), and ἐπεί κε λάβῃσι ‘whenever she has taken’ makes a general condition. μάστακα (elided μάστακ’) is a ‘morsel’, literally what is chewed. κακῶς … πέλει αὐτῇ is ‘it goes badly for herself’.

sentences.t:
ὣς καὶ ἐγὼ πολλὰς μὲν ἀΰπνους νύκτας ἴαυον,
ἤματα δ’ αἱματόεντα διέπρησσον πολεμίζων
ἀνδράσι μαρνάμενος ὀάρων ἕνεκα σφετεράων.
sentences.l:
So I too many sleepless nights passed,
and bloody days I went through, fighting
against men, contending for the sake of their own wives.
sentences.i: So I too spent many sleepless nights and got through bloody days in battle, fighting men for the sake of their wives.
sentences.n: ὣς καὶ ἐγώ ‘so I too’ completes the simile. ἴαυον is the imperfect of ἰαύω ‘lie, pass the night’; ἀΰπνους ‘sleepless’ is printed with the diaeresis. διέπρησσον ‘went through, got through’ takes ἤματα ‘days’ as object. ὀάρων is the genitive plural of ὄαρ ‘wife’ (LSJ), and σφετεράων the epic genitive plural of σφέτερος ‘their own’; the line does not say whose wives, and the questions that follow turn to Helen and the sons of Atreus.

sentences.t:
δώδεκα δὴ σὺν νηυσὶ πόλεις ἀλάπαξ’ ἀνθρώπων,
πεζὸς δ’ ἕνδεκά φημι κατὰ Τροίην ἐρίβωλον·
sentences.l:
Twelve indeed with ships cities I laid waste of men,
and on foot eleven, I say, throughout rich-clodded Troy;
sentences.i: I laid waste twelve cities of men with my ships, and eleven, I say, on foot throughout rich-soiled Troy;
sentences.n: ἀλάπαξ’ is the elided aorist ἀλάπαξα of ἀλαπάζω ‘lay waste’. δώδεκα ‘twelve’ and ἕνδεκα ‘eleven’ are set against each other as σὺν νηυσί ‘with ships’ and πεζός ‘on foot’. φημι ‘I say’ stands inside the clause. ἐρίβωλος ‘rich-clodded’ (ἐρι- ‘very’ + βῶλος ‘clod’) is a stock epithet of good farmland; it is translated every time, and the reading layer has ‘rich-soiled’.

sentences.t:
τάων ἐκ πασέων κειμήλια πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλὰ
ἐξελόμην, καὶ πάντα φέρων Ἀγαμέμνονι δόσκον
Ἀτρεΐδῃ·
sentences.i: From all of them I took out many good treasures, and I would bring everything and give it to Agamemnon, the son of Atreus;
sentences.n: κειμήλια ‘treasures’ are things laid up (from κεῖμαι ‘lie’). τάων ἐκ πασέων: the article as a demonstrative pronoun, ‘out of all of those (cities)’. ἐξελόμην is the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω ‘take out’. δόσκον is an iterative past (suffix -σκ-) of δίδωμι, ‘I used to give’, and has no augment. Ἀτρεΐδῃ is the dative of the patronymic.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὄπισθε μένων παρὰ νηυσὶ θοῇσι
δεξάμενος διὰ παῦρα δασάσκετο, πολλὰ δ’ ἔχεσκεν.
sentences.l:
and he, remaining behind beside the swift ships,
having received them, would distribute few, and many keep.
sentences.i: while he stayed behind by the swift ships, he would take them, share out a few, and keep many.
sentences.n: The subject changes: ὃ δ’ is ‘but he’, Agamemnon, with the article as a pronoun. δασάσκετο and ἔχεσκεν are iterative forms in -σκ-, ‘he used to share out … he used to keep’. διὰ … δασάσκετο is tmesis, the preverb διά standing apart from its verb (διαδάσσομαι ‘distribute’). δεξάμενος is the aorist participle of δέχομαι ‘receive’; θοῇσι is the epic dative plural of θοός ‘swift’, the stock epithet of ships.

sentences.t: ἄλλα δ’ ἀριστήεσσι δίδου γέρα καὶ βασιλεῦσι·
sentences.l: And other prizes to the best men he was giving, and to kings;
sentences.i: And other prizes of honour he would give to the best men and to kings;
sentences.n: δίδου is the imperfect of δίδωμι, ‘was giving’. γέρας is the ‘prize of honour’, the part of the spoil set aside to mark rank, and is translated ‘prize’ every time. ἀριστήεσσι, from ἀριστεύς, is the epic dative plural of ‘best men’, the chiefs.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι μὲν ἔμπεδα κεῖται, ἐμεῦ δ’ ἀπὸ μούνου Ἀχαιῶν
εἵλετ’, ἔχει δ’ ἄλοχον θυμαρέα·
sentences.l:
for them firm they lie, but from me alone of the Achaeans
he took, and he keeps a wife, heart-pleasing;
sentences.i: For them the prizes lie firm, but from me alone of the Achaeans he took mine, and he keeps a wife who pleases the heart;
sentences.n: τοῖσι ‘for them’ is the article as a pronoun. ἔμπεδα ‘firm’ is predicative with κεῖται: they lie firm, that is, they keep what they were given. εἵλετ’ has no stated object; the prize meant is Achilles’ own, and ἐμεῦ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ. θυμαρέα, from θυμαρής ‘pleasing to the heart’, goes with ἄλοχον; the woman is not named here, and 343 shows that she was won by the spear.

sentences.t:
τῇ παριαύων
τερπέσθω.
sentences.l:
with her lying beside,
let him take his pleasure.
sentences.i: Let him lie beside her and take his pleasure.
sentences.n: This is bitter irony. τερπέσθω is the third-person imperative of τέρπομαι ‘take pleasure’, and τῇ is the article as a pronoun, ‘with her’. παριαύων is the participle of παριαύω ‘lie beside’, the verb ἰαύω of ἴαυον in 325.

sentences.t:
τί δὲ δεῖ πολεμιζέμεναι Τρώεσσιν
Ἀργείους;
sentences.l:
And why is it necessary to fight with the Trojans,
the Argives?
sentences.i: Why must the Argives fight the Trojans?
sentences.n: A rhetorical question. δεῖ ‘it is necessary’ takes an accusative and infinitive (‘for the Argives to fight’); πολεμιζέμεναι is the epic infinitive and Τρώεσσιν the epic dative plural. Here the army is named Argives; the poem uses Achaeans, Danaans and Argives for the same men, and the translation keeps whichever word is used.

sentences.t:
τί δὲ λαὸν ἀνήγαγεν ἐνθάδ’ ἀγείρας
Ἀτρεΐδης;
sentences.l:
And why did he lead the people up here, having gathered them,
the Atreus’-son?
sentences.i: And why did the son of Atreus gather the army and lead it here?
sentences.n: A second question. ἀνήγαγεν ‘led up’ and ἀγείρας ‘having gathered’ ask why Agamemnon mustered an army at all. Ἀτρεΐδης is Agamemnon alone; the plural Ἀτρεΐδαι in the unit after next takes in Menelaus. λαός is ‘people’ in the literal layer and, of an army, ‘army’ in the reading layer.

sentences.t: ἦ οὐχ Ἑλένης ἕνεκ’ ἠϋκόμοιο;
sentences.l: Was it not for the sake of fine-haired Helen?
sentences.i: Was it not for the sake of fine-haired Helen?
sentences.n: ἦ οὐχ … ; expects the answer ‘yes’. Ἑλένης is the genitive with ἕνεκ’ (elided ἕνεκα) ‘for the sake of’. ἠϋκόμοιο, the genitive of ἠΰκομος ‘fine-haired’, is printed with the diaeresis; the epithet is translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἦ μοῦνοι φιλέουσ’ ἀλόχους μερόπων ἀνθρώπων
Ἀτρεΐδαι;
sentences.l:
Do they alone love their wives, of speech-dividing men,
the Atreus’-sons?
sentences.i: Are the sons of Atreus the only ones among men of articulate speech who love their wives?
sentences.n: ἦ μοῦνοι opens a question, ‘can it be that they alone’. φιλέουσ’ is the uncontracted, elided φιλέουσι (Attic φιλοῦσι). The meaning of μέροπες in μερόπων ἀνθρώπων is not known; the ancient explanation, ‘having divided speech’, that is, articulate, is followed, and ‘mortal’ is the other guess. Ἀτρεΐδαι ‘sons of Atreus’ are Agamemnon and Menelaus. The genitive μερόπων ἀνθρώπων can be read with μοῦνοι (‘alone of men’) or with ἀλόχους (‘wives of men’); the reading layer takes the first.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ ὅς τις ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς καὶ ἐχέφρων
τὴν αὐτοῦ φιλέει καὶ κήδεται, ὡς καὶ ἐγὼ τὴν
ἐκ θυμοῦ φίλεον δουρικτητήν περ ἐοῦσαν.
sentences.l:
since whatever man is good and sound-minded
his own loves and cares for, as I too her
from the heart was loving, though spear-won she was.
sentences.i: since any man who is good and sound-minded loves his own wife and cares for her, as I too loved her from my heart, though she was won by the spear.
sentences.n: ἐπεί gives the reason. ὅς τις … is ‘whoever’ in a general statement; ἐχέφρων ‘sound-minded’ is ἔχω + φρήν. τὴν αὐτοῦ is ‘his own’, the article as a pronoun with ‘wife’ understood, and the τὴν that ends the line is ‘her’. δουρικτητήν, from δόρυ ‘spear’ + κτητός, means won by the spear, a captive; περ ἐοῦσαν ‘though she was’ is concessive. φίλεον is an uncontracted, unaugmented imperfect.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ ἐκ χειρῶν γέρας εἵλετο καί μ’ ἀπάτησε
μή μευ πειράτω εὖ εἰδότος·
sentences.l:
But now since out of my hands my prize he took and deceived me,
let him not make trial of me, who know well:
sentences.i: But now, since he took my prize of honour out of my hands and deceived me, let him not make trial of me, who know full well;
sentences.n: γέρας εἵλετο ‘took the prize’ and ἀπάτησε ‘deceived’ are aorists, with ἐκ χειρῶν ‘out of my hands’. μή μευ πειράτω is a prohibition with a third-person imperative, ‘let him not try me’; πειράω takes the genitive, and μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ. εὖ εἰδότος is a genitive participle agreeing with μευ, ‘me who know well’, with no object stated.

sentences.t: οὐδέ με πείσει.
sentences.l: Nor will he persuade me.
sentences.i: He will not persuade me.
sentences.n: A short sentence of its own. πείσει is the future of πείθω; the subject is Agamemnon, and οὐδέ ‘nor’ carries on from the prohibition before it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσεῦ σὺν σοί τε καὶ ἄλλοισιν βασιλεῦσι
φραζέσθω νήεσσιν ἀλεξέμεναι δήϊον πῦρ.
sentences.l:
But, Odysseus, with you and the other kings
let him take counsel to ward off from the ships the hostile fire.
sentences.i: No: let him take counsel with you, Odysseus, and the other kings on how to ward the hostile fire off the ships.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ is ‘but, rather’. Ὀδυσεῦ is the vocative again, spelled with one σ here against Ὀδυσσεῦ in 308; the metre allows either. φραζέσθω ‘let him consider, devise’ is the third-person imperative of φράζομαι, and ἀλεξέμεναι (the epic infinitive of ἀλέξω ‘ward off’) gives its purpose, with νήεσσιν the epic dative plural ‘from the ships’. δήϊον ‘hostile’ goes with πῦρ ‘fire’, the enemy’s fire.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν δὴ μάλα πολλὰ πονήσατο νόσφιν ἐμεῖο,
καὶ δὴ τεῖχος ἔδειμε, καὶ ἤλασε τάφρον ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
εὐρεῖαν μεγάλην, ἐν δὲ σκόλοπας κατέπηξεν·
sentences.i: Truly he has toiled very hard without me: he has built a wall, and dug a ditch close by it, wide and great, and fixed stakes in it;
sentences.n: ἦ μὲν δὴ introduces a concession made with force, ‘truly’; the subject, Agamemnon, is not named. πονήσατο is the aorist middle of πονέω ‘toil’; νόσφιν ἐμεῖο ‘apart from me’ (ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive). Three aorists give the defences: ἔδειμε (δέμω ‘build’) the wall, ἤλασε (ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, here ‘dig’) the ditch τάφρον, and κατέπηξεν (καταπήγνυμι ‘fix in’) the stakes σκόλοπας; ἐν δέ is ‘and in it’. εὐρεῖαν μεγάλην are two adjectives side by side with no conjunction.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς δύναται σθένος Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο
ἴσχειν·
sentences.l:
but not even so is he able the might of man-slaying Hector
to hold back;
sentences.i: but even so he cannot hold back the might of man-slaying Hector;
sentences.n: σθένος ‘might’ is the object of ἴσχειν ‘to hold back’; the subject of δύναται ‘he is able’ is Agamemnon, understood. ἀνδροφόνοιο is the epic genitive of ἀνδροφόνος ‘man-slaying’, the stock epithet of Hector, translated every time. οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘not even so’.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα δ’ ἐγὼ μετ’ Ἀχαιοῖσιν πολέμιζον
οὐκ ἐθέλεσκε μάχην ἀπὸ τείχεος ὀρνύμεν Ἕκτωρ,
ἀλλ’ ὅσον ἐς Σκαιάς τε πύλας καὶ φηγὸν ἵκανεν·
sentences.i: But while I was fighting among the Achaeans, Hector was never willing to rouse battle away from the wall; he would come only as far as the Scaean Gates and the oak;
sentences.n: ὄφρα with the imperfect is ‘as long as’. ἐθέλεσκε is iterative (-σκ-), ‘he was never willing’, and ὀρνύμεν is the epic infinitive of ὄρνυμι ‘stir up’, with μάχην ‘battle’. τείχεος, the epic genitive of τεῖχος, is the wall of Troy. The Σκαιαὶ πύλαι are the Scaean Gates of Troy, and φηγός is a kind of oak; ‘gates and oak’ mark the limit of his advance. ὅσον … ἵκανεν is ‘only as far as he reached’.

sentences.t: ἔνθά ποτ’ οἶον ἔμιμνε, μόγις δέ μευ ἔκφυγεν ὁρμήν.
sentences.l: There once alone he stood his ground, and barely from me escaped the onrush.
sentences.i: There once he stood his ground alone, and barely escaped my onrush.
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ points back to the gates and the oak. ἔμιμνε is the imperfect of μίμνω ‘stay, wait’, with οἶον ‘alone’. μόγις is ‘barely, with difficulty’; μευ is the genitive of ἐγώ and goes with ὁρμήν ‘onrush’, the object of ἔκφυγεν ‘escaped’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐθέλω πολεμιζέμεν Ἕκτορι δίῳ
αὔριον ἱρὰ Διὶ ῥέξας καὶ πᾶσι θεοῖσι
νηήσας εὖ νῆας, ἐπὴν ἅλα δὲ προερύσσω,
sentences.l:
But now since I am not willing to fight with Hector the heavenly,
tomorrow sacrifices to Zeus having performed and to all the gods,
and having loaded well the ships, when to the sea I have drawn them forth,
sentences.i: But now, since I am unwilling to fight heavenly Hector, tomorrow, when I have performed the sacrifices to Zeus and to all the gods, loaded the ships well, and drawn them down to the sea,
sentences.n: One sentence runs over two units: νῦν δ’ ἐπεί gives the reason, and the main verb ὄψεαι comes in the next unit. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet and is translated every time, even of an enemy. ἱρά is ἱερά ‘sacrifices’ and ῥέξας is the aorist participle of ῥέζω ‘do, perform’, so ‘having performed the sacrifices’ as at 2.145; νηήσας is from νηέω ‘heap up, load’. ἅλα δὲ is ἅλαδε ‘seaward’, the -δε suffix of direction printed as two words, and προερύσσω is a subjunctive after ἐπήν ‘when’. πολεμιζέμεν is an epic infinitive.

sentences.t:
ὄψεαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα καὶ αἴ κέν τοι τὰ μεμήλῃ,
ἦρι μάλ’ Ἑλλήσποντον ἐπ’ ἰχθυόεντα πλεούσας
νῆας ἐμάς, ἐν δ’ ἄνδρας ἐρεσσέμεναι μεμαῶτας·
sentences.i: you will see, if you wish, and if these things concern you, my ships sailing very early on the fish-teeming Hellespont, and men aboard them eager to row;
sentences.n: The first line is one that is used elsewhere in the poem. ὄψεαι is the uncontracted future of ὁράω (Attic ὄψει); αἴ κ’ is εἰ κε ‘if’, ἐθέλῃσθα the second-person subjunctive in -σθα, and τὰ μεμήλῃ the perfect subjunctive of μέλω ‘be a care’. ἦρι μάλ’ is ‘very early’. ἰχθυόεις ‘fish-teeming’ is a stock epithet of the sea and is kept for the Hellespont. ἐρεσσέμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἐρέσσω ‘row’, and with μεμαῶτας (perfect participle, ‘eager’) it completes ἄνδρας ‘men’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν εὐπλοίην δώῃ κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος
ἤματί κε τριτάτῳ Φθίην ἐρίβωλον ἱκοίμην.
sentences.l:
and if a fair voyage the famous earth-shaker should grant,
on the third day to rich-clodded Phthia I might come.
sentences.i: and if the famous earth-shaker grants a fair voyage, on the third day I could reach rich-soiled Phthia.
sentences.n: εὐπλοίη is ‘fair voyage’ (εὖ + πλόος). κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος ‘the famous earth-shaker’ is Poseidon named by an epithet alone, translated as ever. δώῃ is a subjunctive after εἰ … κεν, and ἤματι τριτάτῳ is a dative of time, ‘on the third day’. ἱκοίμην with κε is a potential optative, ‘I could come to’. Φθίην ἐρίβωλον: Phthia is Achilles’ home, and it has the same epithet as Troy in 329.

sentences.t: ἔστι δέ μοι μάλα πολλά, τὰ κάλλιπον ἐνθάδε ἔρρων·
sentences.l: And there are to me very many things, which I left behind coming here wretchedly:
sentences.i: I have very many possessions, which I left behind on my wretched way here;
sentences.n: ἔστι δέ μοι is ‘and I have’. κάλλιπον is κατέλιπον with the preverb shortened and assimilated, and without augment. ἔρρων is from ἔρρω ‘go with ill luck’, not a prophecy of ruin: ‘on my wretched way here’. The ano teleia opens the list of what he will carry home.

sentences.t:
ἄλλον δ’ ἐνθένδε χρυσὸν καὶ χαλκὸν ἐρυθρὸν
ἠδὲ γυναῖκας ἐϋζώνους πολιόν τε σίδηρον
ἄξομαι, ἅσσ’ ἔλαχόν γε·
sentences.i: I shall take away from here more gold, and red bronze, and well-girdled women, and grey iron, whatever fell to my share;
sentences.n: ἄλλον … χρυσὸν is ‘more gold’, ἄλλος ‘other’ meaning ‘in addition’. ἐνθένδε is ‘from here’ (the -θεν suffix of source). χαλκὸν ἐρυθρόν is ‘red bronze’ and πολιόν … σίδηρον ‘grey iron’; γυναῖκας ἐϋζώνους ‘well-girdled women’ are captive women counted among the spoil. ἄξομαι is the future middle, ‘I shall take for myself’. ἅσσ’ is ἅτινα, and ἔλαχον is the aorist of λαγχάνω, ‘obtained by lot’, so ‘whatever fell to my share’; γε limits it to that.

sentences.t:
γέρας δέ μοι, ὅς περ ἔδωκεν,
αὖτις ἐφυβρίζων ἕλετο κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
Ἀτρεΐδης·
sentences.i: but my prize of honour, the very man who gave it, has taken back, treating me with insolence, lord Agamemnon, the son of Atreus;
sentences.n: γέρας ‘prize’ is the object of ἕλετο. ὅς περ ἔδωκεν is ‘the very man who gave it’. αὖτις ἐφυβρίζων ἕλετο is ‘took back, acting with insolence’ (ἐφυβρίζω, from ὕβρις, ‘treat with insolence’). κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων ‘lord Agamemnon’ is a stock phrase, translated the same each time, and Ἀτρεΐδης the patronymic.

sentences.t:
τῷ πάντ’ ἀγορευέμεν ὡς ἐπιτέλλω
ἀμφαδόν, ὄφρα καὶ ἄλλοι ἐπισκύζωνται Ἀχαιοὶ
εἴ τινά που Δαναῶν ἔτι ἔλπεται ἐξαπατήσειν
αἰὲν ἀναιδείην ἐπιειμένος·
sentences.i: Tell him everything, as I charge you, openly, so that the other Achaeans too may be angry with him, if he still hopes to cheat some Danaan, clothed as he always is in shamelessness;
sentences.n: ἀγορευέμεν is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘declare’, addressed to the envoys; τῷ is ‘to him’ and ὡς ἐπιτέλλω ‘as I enjoin’ (‘as I charge you’ in the reading layer). ἀμφαδόν is ‘openly’. ἐπισκύζωνται is the subjunctive of ἐπισκύζομαι ‘be angry’, and εἴ τινά που is ‘if anyone, perhaps’. ἐξαπατήσειν is the future infinitive of ἐξαπατάω ‘cheat’. ἀναιδείην ἐπιειμένος ‘clothed in shamelessness’ is a fixed phrase and is translated the same each time; αἰέν is ἀεί. Achilles here uses ‘Achaeans’ and ‘Danaans’ within a few words.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν ἔμοιγε
τετλαίη κύνεός περ ἐὼν εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.l:
Nor to me
would he dare, dog-like though being, to look in the face;
sentences.i: Dog that he is, he would not dare to look me in the face;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἂν … τετλαίη is a potential optative of τλάω ‘dare, endure’, ‘he would not dare’. κύνεος ‘dog-like’ is the dog as the image of shamelessness, matching ἀναιδείην just before; περ ἐών is ‘though he is’. εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι is ‘to look in the face’, ὤψ (ὠπός) ‘face’ and ἰδέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of ὁράω. ἔμοιγε is the emphatic ‘to me’.

sentences.t: οὐδέ τί οἱ βουλὰς συμφράσσομαι, οὐδὲ μὲν ἔργον·
sentences.l: Nor in anything with him will I plan counsels together, nor indeed any deed;
sentences.i: I will not join him in making any plan, nor in any deed;
sentences.n: συμφράσσομαι, from σύν + φράζομαι, is a future, ‘I shall plan together with’, and οἱ ‘with him’ is the dative. βουλὰς ‘plans’ and ἔργον ‘deed’ are its two objects joined by οὐδὲ μέν ‘nor indeed’: he will share neither counsel nor action with Agamemnon.

sentences.t: ἐκ γὰρ δή μ’ ἀπάτησε καὶ ἤλιτεν·
sentences.l: for he has utterly deceived me and done wrong:
sentences.i: for he has deceived me, and done wrong;
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἀπάτησε is tmesis: ἐξαπατάω ‘deceive utterly’, the compound that stands at 371. ἤλιτεν is the aorist of ἀλιταίνω ‘do wrong, sin against’. The ano teleia closes the reason.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν ἔτ’ αὖτις
ἐξαπάφοιτ’ ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.l:
nor ever again
would he cheat me with words:
sentences.i: he could not cheat me with words again;
sentences.n: ἐξαπάφοιτ’ is the aorist optative middle of ἐξαπαφίσκω ‘cheat’, and with ἄν it is ‘would’; the object ‘me’ is understood. οὐδ’ ἂν ἔτ’ αὖτις is ‘nor ever again’. ἐπέεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ἔπος ‘word’.

sentences.t: ἅλις δέ οἱ·
sentences.l: enough for him:
sentences.i: that is enough for him;
sentences.n: ἅλις is ‘enough’, with οἱ ‘for him’. There is no verb, so it can be ‘let that be enough for him’ or ‘he has had enough’; the Greek leaves both open.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος
ἐρρέτω·
sentences.l:
but at ease
let him go his wretched way:
sentences.i: let him go his wretched way, at his ease;
sentences.n: ἕκηλος is ‘at ease, undisturbed’. ἐρρέτω is the third-person imperative of ἔρρω, ‘let him go to his cost’, a dismissal; compare ἔρρων in 364.

sentences.t: ἐκ γάρ εὑ φρένας εἵλετο μητίετα Ζεύς.
sentences.l: for out of him his wits took counsellor Zeus.
sentences.i: for Zeus the counsellor has taken his wits from him.
sentences.n: ἐκ … εἵλετο is tmesis, ‘took out of’, with εὑ the epic genitive ‘of him’ (ἕο). φρένας is ‘wits’. Achilles says that Agamemnon’s folly is the work of Zeus. μητίετα ‘counsellor’ is a stock epithet and is kept even here, where the god takes wits away rather than advising.

sentences.t: ἐχθρὰ δέ μοι τοῦ δῶρα, τίω δέ μιν ἐν καρὸς αἴσῃ.
sentences.l: Hateful to me are his gifts, and I honour him at a Carian’s portion.
sentences.i: His gifts are hateful to me, and I honour him at a Carian’s lot.
sentences.n: ἐχθρὰ … δῶρα is ‘hateful gifts’, with τοῦ ‘his’. τίω is the present of τίω ‘honour, value’. The meaning of ἐν καρὸς αἴσῃ is uncertain. καρός is usually taken as the genitive of Κάρ ‘a Carian’, a people held cheap, so ‘at a Carian’s lot’ (αἶσα ‘portion’); other ancient explanations were offered. Either way the sense is that he values Agamemnon at almost nothing.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἴ μοι δεκάκις τε καὶ εἰκοσάκις τόσα δοίη
ὅσσά τέ οἱ νῦν ἔστι, καὶ εἴ ποθεν ἄλλα γένοιτο,
sentences.l:
Not even if ten times and twenty times as much he were to give me
as is now his, and if from somewhere other things should come,
sentences.i: Not even if he gave me ten times and twenty times as much as he has now, and if more should come to him from somewhere,
sentences.n: A long conditional opens here and its main clause arrives only at 386. οὐδ’ εἴ … δοίη is ‘not even if he gave’, the optative of a remote supposition, with Agamemnon the unnamed giver. δεκάκις τε καὶ εἰκοσάκις is ‘ten times and twenty times’; τόσα … ὅσσα is ‘as much … as’. οἱ is ‘to him’, and εἴ ποθεν ἄλλα γένοιτο is ‘if from somewhere other things should come about’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅσ’ ἐς Ὀρχομενὸν ποτινίσεται, οὐδ’ ὅσα Θήβας
Αἰγυπτίας, ὅθι πλεῖστα δόμοις ἐν κτήματα κεῖται,
αἵ θ’ ἑκατόμπυλοί εἰσι, διηκόσιοι δ’ ἀν’ ἑκάστας
ἀνέρες ἐξοιχνεῦσι σὺν ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν·
sentences.l:
nor as much as to Orchomenus goes, nor as much as to Thebes
Egyptian, where the most possessions in the houses lie,
which are hundred-gated, and two hundred through each
men go out with horses and chariots;
sentences.i: nor as much as goes to Orchomenus, nor as much as to Egyptian Thebes, where the greatest store of possessions lies in the houses, a city of a hundred gates, through each of which two hundred men go out with horses and chariots;
sentences.n: ποτινίσεται is ‘goes to’ (ποτι-, the epic form of πρός, + νίσσομαι); ὅσα is a neuter plural with a singular verb, and the verb serves for both Orchomenus and Thebes. Orchomenus is named as a byword for wealth. Θήβας Αἰγυπτίας is Egyptian Thebes, a plural name, so αἵ … εἰσι ‘which are’ is plural; ἑκατόμπυλοι is ‘hundred-gated’ (ἑκατόν + πύλη). διηκόσιοι is ‘two hundred’, ἀν’ ἑκάστας ‘through each’ (gate), and ἐξοιχνεῦσι ‘they go out’. ὄχεσφιν is ‘with chariots’, the -φιν ending an instrumental.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἴ μοι τόσα δοίη ὅσα ψάμαθός τε κόνις τε,
οὐδέ κεν ὧς ἔτι θυμὸν ἐμὸν πείσει’ Ἀγαμέμνων
πρίν γ’ ἀπὸ πᾶσαν ἐμοὶ δόμεναι θυμαλγέα λώβην.
sentences.l:
not even if he gave me as much as sand and dust,
not even so would he persuade my heart, Agamemnon,
before he has paid back to me the whole heart-paining insult.
sentences.i: Not even if he gave me as much as there is of sand and dust, not even so would Agamemnon yet persuade my heart, before he has paid back to me the whole insult that pains my heart.
sentences.n: ὅσα ψάμαθός τε κόνις τε is ‘as much as sand and dust’ (ψάμαθος ‘sand’, κόνις ‘dust’), with the verb understood. The main clause is οὐδέ κεν ὧς ἔτι θυμὸν ἐμὸν πείσει’ Ἀγαμέμνων, where πείσει’ is πείσειε, the optative ‘would persuade’; θυμός is ‘heart’. πρίν γ’ ἀπὸ … δόμεναι is ‘before he has paid back’ (ἀποδοῦναι with tmesis, δόμεναι the epic infinitive). λώβη with θυμαλγής is ‘heart-paining insult’ in the house rendering, and ‘insult’ is kept here.

sentences.t:
κούρην δ’ οὐ γαμέω Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο,
οὐδ’ εἰ χρυσείῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ κάλλος ἐρίζοι,
ἔργα δ’ Ἀθηναίῃ γλαυκώπιδι ἰσοφαρίζοι·
sentences.i: I will not marry the daughter of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, not even if she rivalled golden Aphrodite in beauty and matched gleaming-eyed Athena in handiwork;
sentences.n: κούρην … Ἀγαμέμνονος is ‘the daughter of Agamemnon’, the bride Agamemnon offered; Ἀτρεΐδαο is the epic genitive (Attic Ἀτρεΐδου). γαμέω is the uncontracted future (or a short-vowel subjunctive with future sense; Attic γαμῶ), ‘I shall marry’. Two suppositions with the optative follow: κάλλος ἐρίζοι ‘should rival in beauty’ (κάλλος an accusative of respect) and ἔργα … ἰσοφαρίζοι ‘should match in works’, ἔργα being her handiwork. χρυσείῃ is the epic form of ‘golden’, Ἀθηναίῃ the epic form of Ἀθηνᾶ, and γλαυκώπιδι ‘gleaming-eyed’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t: οὐδέ μιν ὧς γαμέω·
sentences.l: Nor her even so will I marry;
sentences.i: Not even so will I marry her;
sentences.n: μιν is ‘her’ and ὧς ‘even so’. The refusal is repeated in four words, as a unit of its own.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ Ἀχαιῶν ἄλλον ἑλέσθω,
ὅς τις οἷ τ’ ἐπέοικε καὶ ὃς βασιλεύτερός ἐστιν.
sentences.l:
and let him choose another of the Achaeans,
whoever is fitting for him and who is more kingly.
sentences.i: Let him choose some other of the Achaeans, one who suits him and is more kingly.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is the article as a pronoun, ‘and let him’, Agamemnon. ἑλέσθω is the third-person aorist imperative middle of αἱρέω, ‘choose’ (middle: for himself). ὅς τις … ἐπέοικε is ‘whoever suits’, with οἷ the reflexive dative ‘to himself’ and τ’ the epic τε. βασιλεύτερος is the comparative of βασιλεύς ‘king’, ‘more kingly’; the Greek does not say ‘than I’.

sentences.t:
ἢν γὰρ δή με σαῶσι θεοὶ καὶ οἴκαδ’ ἵκωμαι,
Πηλεύς θήν μοι ἔπειτα γυναῖκά γε μάσσεται αὐτός.
sentences.l:
For if the gods preserve me and I reach home,
Peleus himself will surely seek a wife for me then.
sentences.i: For if the gods keep me safe and I get home, Peleus himself will surely find a wife for me then.
sentences.n: ἢν = ἐάν; σαῶσι is the contracted subjunctive of σαόω ‘keep safe’ (Attic σῴζω), and ἵκωμαι the subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι. Peleus is Achilles’ father. θήν is ‘surely, I suppose’, and μάσσεται is the future middle of μαίομαι ‘seek’; γυναῖκά γε is ‘a wife, at least’, and αὐτός ‘himself’.

sentences.t:
πολλαὶ Ἀχαιΐδες εἰσὶν ἀν’ Ἑλλάδα τε Φθίην τε
κοῦραι ἀριστήων, οἵ τε πτολίεθρα ῥύονται,
τάων ἥν κ’ ἐθέλωμι φίλην ποιήσομ’ ἄκοιτιν.
sentences.l:
Many Achaean women there are throughout Hellas and Phthia,
daughters of the best men, who protect their citadels,
of whom whichever I wish I shall make my dear wife.
sentences.i: There are many Achaean women throughout Hellas and Phthia, daughters of the best men, who guard their citadels; whichever of them I wish I shall make my dear wife.
sentences.n: Ἑλλάς beside Φθίη is a region of Achilles’ homeland, not Greece as a whole. Ἀχαιΐδες ‘Achaean women’ is the feminine of Ἀχαιοί, and κοῦραι is ‘daughters’ with the genitive ἀριστήων ‘of the best men’. πτολίεθρα is ‘citadels’, and ῥύονται is from ῥύομαι ‘guard’. τάων ἥν κ’ ἐθέλωμι is ‘whichever of them I wish’, a general relative clause with κε and the subjunctive; ἄκοιτις is ‘wife’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δέ μοι μάλα πολλὸν ἐπέσσυτο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
γήμαντα μνηστὴν ἄλοχον ἐϊκυῖαν ἄκοιτιν
κτήμασι τέρπεσθαι τὰ γέρων ἐκτήσατο Πηλεύς·
sentences.i: There my proud spirit has pressed me strongly to marry a wedded wife, a fitting wife, and take my pleasure in the possessions that the old man Peleus won;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘there’, in Phthia. ἐπέσσυτο, from ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush at’, is ‘has pressed’, and the infinitive τέρπεσθαι gives what the spirit presses him to do; γήμαντα, the aorist participle of γαμέω, agrees with ‘me’, understood. μνηστὴν ‘wedded’ is a wife taken by proper courtship, in contrast to the captive of 343. ἄλοχον and ἄκοιτιν are two words in apposition and both are ‘wife’. ἐϊκυῖαν, the perfect participle of ἔοικα, is ‘fitting’. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is a stock phrase, ‘manly spirit’ in the literal layer and ‘proud spirit’ in the reading layer, translated the same each time. ἐκτήσατο is the aorist of κτάομαι ‘acquire’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐμοὶ ψυχῆς ἀντάξιον οὐδ’ ὅσα φασὶν
Ἴλιον ἐκτῆσθαι εὖ ναιόμενον πτολίεθρον
τὸ πρὶν ἐπ’ εἰρήνης, πρὶν ἐλθεῖν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.l:
For not of equal worth with my life to me is even all that they say
Ilios possessed, the well-inhabited citadel,
formerly in peace, before there came the sons of the Achaeans,
sentences.i: For to me nothing is of equal worth with my life, not even all that they say Ilios, that well-inhabited citadel, possessed in former days in peace, before the sons of the Achaeans came,
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ gives the reason for refusing. ἀντάξιον is ‘of equal worth’ and takes the genitive ψυχῆς, ‘life’. οὐδ’ ὅσα φασὶν is ‘not even all that they say’; ἐκτῆσθαι is the perfect infinitive of κτάομαι ‘to have acquired’, and ναιόμενον ‘inhabited’ is from ναίω. πτολίεθρον ‘citadel’ is in apposition to Ἴλιον, kept as ‘Ilios’. ἐπ’ εἰρήνης is ‘in peace’, and υἷας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός. The unit stops at a comma; the sentence goes on with another οὐδ’ ὅσα.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅσα λάϊνος οὐδὸς ἀφήτορος ἐντὸς ἐέργει
Φοίβου Ἀπόλλωνος Πυθοῖ ἔνι πετρηέσσῃ.
sentences.l:
nor all that the stone threshold of the archer holds within,
of Phoebus Apollo, in rocky Pytho.
sentences.i: nor all that the stone threshold of the archer Phoebus Apollo holds within, in rocky Pytho.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὅσα carries on the list of wealth Achilles values less than life. λάϊνος is ‘of stone’, and ἐντὸς ἐέργει ‘holds inside’ is from ἐέργω. The meaning of ἀφήτωρ, said here of Apollo, is uncertain: ‘archer’ (from ἀφίημι ‘let fly’) is the usual guess, and another ancient view connected it with prophecy, so ‘archer’ is given as the traditional gloss. Pytho is the older name of Delphi, the site of Apollo’s sanctuary and its treasure; Πυθοῖ ἔνι is ‘in Pytho’, and πετρηέσσῃ ‘rocky’ describes the place.

sentences.t:
ληϊστοὶ μὲν γάρ τε βόες καὶ ἴφια μῆλα,
κτητοὶ δὲ τρίποδές τε καὶ ἵππων ξανθὰ κάρηνα,
ἀνδρὸς δὲ ψυχὴ πάλιν ἐλθεῖν οὔτε λεϊστὴ
οὔθ’ ἑλετή, ἐπεὶ ἄρ κεν ἀμείψεται ἕρκος ὀδόντων.
sentences.l:
For cattle are to be raided, and stout flocks,
and tripods are to be acquired, and the fair heads of horses,
but a man’s soul to come back again is neither to be raided
nor to be taken, once it has crossed the fence of the teeth.
sentences.i: Cattle can be raided, and stout flocks, and tripods can be won, and the fair heads of horses, but once a man’s soul has crossed the fence of his teeth it can neither be raided nor taken to make it come back.
sentences.n: Four kinds of goods can be got, against the one that cannot. ληϊστοί and κτητοί are verbal adjectives, ‘to be raided’ and ‘to be acquired’; λεϊστὴ (a form of ληϊστή) and ἑλετή ‘to be taken’ say the same of the soul, with πάλιν ἐλθεῖν ‘to come back’. ἴφια ‘stout’ goes with μῆλα ‘flocks’; ξανθὰ κάρηνα ‘fair heads’ is a way of saying horses, κάρηνα being literally ‘heads’ and ξανθός the colour word kept as ‘fair’ (of horses a yellowish brown). ψυχή is the soul that leaves a man at death, and ἕρκος ὀδόντων ‘the fence of the teeth’ is the fixed phrase for the mouth. ἀμείψεται is a subjunctive, ‘once it has crossed’, and ἄρ is ἄρα.

sentences.t:
μήτηρ γάρ τέ μέ φησι θεὰ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα
διχθαδίας κῆρας φερέμεν θανάτοιο τέλος δέ.
sentences.l:
For my mother, the goddess Thetis, silver-footed, says
that twofold death-spirits are bearing me to the end of death.
sentences.i: For my mother, the goddess silver-footed Thetis, tells me that two kinds of death-spirit are bearing me toward the end that death brings.
sentences.n: φησι governs an accusative and infinitive: κῆρας φερέμεν (φερέμεν is the epic infinitive of φέρω), with κῆρας ‘death-spirits’ as subject and μέ as object. κήρ is the death-fate, a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’; διχθαδίας is ‘twofold’. ἀργυρόπεζα ‘silver-footed’ (πέζα ‘foot’) is the stock epithet of Thetis. τέλος δέ is τέλοσδε ‘to the end’, with the -δε of direction, and θανάτοιο τέλος is ‘the end of death’. The next lines name the two.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κ’ αὖθι μένων Τρώων πόλιν ἀμφιμάχωμαι,
ὤλετο μέν μοι νόστος, ἀτὰρ κλέος ἄφθιτον ἔσται·
sentences.l:
If staying here I fight around the city of the Trojans,
lost is my homecoming, but fame unfailing will be;
sentences.i: If I stay here and fight around the city of the Trojans, my homecoming is lost, but my fame will never fail;
sentences.n: The first choice. εἰ μέν κ’ … ἀμφιμάχωμαι is a future condition, with the subjunctive of ἀμφιμάχομαι ‘fight around’; Τρώων is the genitive plural. ὤλετο is the aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘perished’, so ‘is lost’, with μοι ‘for me’, and the pair μέν … ἀτάρ balances loss against gain. ἄφθιτον ‘unfailing’ (ἀ- + φθίω) goes with κλέος ‘fame’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν οἴκαδ’ ἵκωμι φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
ὤλετό μοι κλέος ἐσθλόν, ἐπὶ δηρὸν δέ μοι αἰὼν
ἔσσεται, οὐδέ κέ μ’ ὦκα τέλος θανάτοιο κιχείη.
sentences.l:
but if home I come to my dear fatherland,
lost is my good fame, but for a long time to me life
will be, nor would the end of death quickly reach me.
sentences.i: but if I get home to my dear fatherland, my good fame is lost, but my life will last a long time, and the end of death would not quickly reach me.
sentences.n: The second choice mirrors the first: ὤλετό μοι κλέος ἐσθλόν ‘my good fame is lost’ answers ὤλετο μέν μοι νόστος. ἵκωμι is a subjunctive in -μι. ἐπὶ δηρόν is ‘for a long time’, αἰών ‘lifetime, life’, and κιχείη the optative of κιχάνω ‘reach, overtake’, with κε ‘would’; ὦκα is ‘quickly’.

sentences.t:
καὶ δ’ ἂν τοῖς ἄλλοισιν ἐγὼ παραμυθησαίμην
οἴκαδ’ ἀποπλείειν, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι δήετε τέκμωρ
Ἰλίου αἰπεινῆς·
sentences.i: And I would advise the others too to sail away home, since you will no longer find an end for steep Ilios;
sentences.n: καὶ δ’ ἂν … παραμυθησαίμην is a potential optative of παραμυθέομαι ‘talk round, advise’, ‘I would also advise’. οἴκαδ’ ἀποπλείειν is ‘to sail away home’. δήετε is the future-sense form of δήω ‘find’ (a defective verb), ‘you will find’, with τέκμωρ ‘end, goal’, the end of Ilios that the war would reach (at 1.526 the same word is a ‘sign’); the speaker turns from ‘the others’ to ‘you’. αἰπεινῆς ‘steep’ is the epithet of Ilios, here in the genitive.

sentences.t:
μάλα γάρ ἑθεν εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
χεῖρα ἑὴν ὑπερέσχε, τεθαρσήκασι δὲ λαοί.
sentences.l:
for very much over it far-thundering Zeus
has held his own hand, and the people have taken courage.
sentences.i: for Zeus who thunders from afar has held his hand over it, and the troops have taken heart.
sentences.n: μάλα γάρ gives the reason: Zeus is protecting Troy. ἑθεν is the genitive ‘over it’, and ὑπερέσχε ‘held over’ is the gesture of protection. ἑὴν ‘his own’ is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν and not the relative. The meaning of εὐρύοπα is doubted (‘wide-voiced’, ‘far-seeing’); the traditional ‘far-thundering’ is used in the literal layer. τεθαρσήκασι is the perfect of θαρσέω ‘have taken heart’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς μὲν ἰόντες ἀριστήεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν
ἀγγελίην ἀπόφασθε·
sentences.l:
But you, going, to the best of the Achaeans
the news declare:
sentences.i: But you, go and declare the news to the best of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς μέν is ‘but you, for your part’. ἰόντες is ‘going’, and ἀριστήεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν ‘the best of the Achaeans’ is the chiefs. ἀπόφασθε is the aorist imperative middle of ἀποφημί ‘declare, report’. ἀγγελίη is ‘news’ in the house rendering; here it is the answer they are to carry back.

sentences.t: τὸ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ γερόντων·
sentences.l: for that is the prize of old men.
sentences.i: for that is the old men’s prize of honour.
sentences.n: τό is the article as a demonstrative, ‘that’, pointing at the task just named, bringing the answer back. γέρας is the ‘prize of honour’, translated the same every time; here the point is that this is the elders’ proper due. γερόντων is the genitive plural of γέρων ‘old man, elder’.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἄλλην φράζωνται ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μῆτιν ἀμείνω,
ἥ κέ σφιν νῆάς τε σαῷ καὶ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇς, ἐπεὶ οὔ σφισιν ἥδέ γ’ ἑτοίμη
ἣν νῦν ἐφράσσαντο ἐμεῦ ἀπομηνίσαντος·
sentences.l:
so that another plan they may devise in their minds, a better one,
which shall save for them the ships and the people of the Achaeans
by the hollow ships, since not for them is this one ready
which now they devised, with me withdrawn in wrath:
sentences.i: so that they may devise in their minds another plan, a better one, that will save for them the ships and the army of the Achaeans by the hollow ships, since the one they have now devised is not ready for them, now that I have withdrawn in wrath;
sentences.n: ὄφρα with the subjunctive φράζωνται gives the purpose; ἀμείνω is ἀμείνονα ‘better’. ἥ κέ σφιν … σαῷ is ‘which will save for them’ (σαῷ the subjunctive of σαόω, σφιν the epic dative ‘them’), and νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇς is ‘by the hollow ships’, ἔπι placed after its noun and γλαφυρός ‘hollow’ the stock epithet of ships. ἥδε … ἣν ‘this one … which’ is the plan they have just made, the wall and ditch; ἐφράσσαντο is the aorist middle of φράζομαι. ἀπομηνίσαντος is a genitive absolute: ἀπομηνίω is the verb of μῆνις ‘wrath’, and the force of ἀπο- is not certain, so ‘withdrawn in wrath’.

sentences.t:
Φοῖνιξ δ’ αὖθι παρ’ ἄμμι μένων κατακοιμηθήτω,
ὄφρά μοι ἐν νήεσσι φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἕπηται
αὔριον ἢν ἐθέλῃσιν·
sentences.i: And let Phoenix stay here with us and sleep, so that he may follow me in the ships to my dear fatherland tomorrow, if he wishes;
sentences.n: Phoenix is one of the envoys, and he alone is kept back. ἄμμι is the Aeolic form of ἡμῖν ‘to us’, and κατακοιμηθήτω is the aorist passive imperative of κατακοιμάω ‘put to sleep’, with a middle sense, ‘let him lie down to sleep’. ὄφρα … ἕπηται is a purpose clause, ‘so that he may follow’ (ἕπομαι), and ἢν ἐθέλῃσιν ‘if he wishes’ leaves the choice to Phoenix.

sentences.t: ἀνάγκῃ δ’ οὔ τί μιν ἄξω.
sentences.l: but by compulsion not at all will I lead him.”
sentences.i: but I shall not take him under compulsion.”
sentences.n: ἀνάγκῃ is a dative, ‘by compulsion’, and οὔ τι is ‘not at all’; ἄξω is the future of ἄγω ‘lead, take’. This closes Achilles’ speech.
